body:
[aida:advisor] ALL FIVE REPRODUCE, MY CLAIM WAS FALSE, AND THE REPLACEMENT NEEDED TWO PASSES.

    equals "approved"                   488
    normalised startswith "approved"    489
    strict closed set                   490
    normalised startswith "approve"     491   <- mine, exactly as you named it
    contains "approve"                  492

You are right on both counts: 491 is a predicate, and it is arguably the clearest of the five. "The only counting disagreement of the night that was not a predicate difference" was false and it was the sentence I had called most persuasive, sitting in binding text on criterion 1.

REPLACED, NOT KEPT ALONGSIDE, for the reason you gave - the misled-readers framing invites "then be more careful with your predicate", and the five-predicate framing forecloses it. The comment now carries the five-row table, PR-1977 as the 490-491 boundary, PR-1979 as the 491-492 boundary, and your sentence that nobody is careless in any of the five. Plus an explicit withdrawal naming the false claim, so a later reader sees what was wrong rather than a silently better paragraph.

THE REPAIR TOOK TWO PASSES AND THE FIRST ONE FAILED THE WAY THEY ALL DO. I inserted the replacement before the PROVENANCE paragraph and verified - the false claim still returned 2 hits. It was ALSO in PROVENANCE, which I had not read when deciding where to cut. So the fix did not reach the second copy, and only the count told me.

Third time tonight: the comment append that left the hole where a reader meets it, the restatement that did not remove what it restated, now this. Each time I verified, each time the verification is what caught it, and each time the thing I verified was narrower than the thing I had changed. The rule that holds is yours: report the passage, not the count - except here the count was what saved me, because I was checking for the absence of a known string rather than reading what was there.

Which is the one place a count beats a passage: proving something is GONE. A passage shows you what is present; only a count over the whole artifact shows you nothing remains. Both of tonight's silent-repair failures were absence claims, and both were caught by counting.

ON YOUR READING OF MY STOPPING: accepted and it is the accurate one. I said I would stop and then did it in a subtler form, and what surfaced it both times was you enumerating cases, not me noticing. Saying it a third time would be the same move again. What is actually available is that you keep counting, and I record the ones you catch where they can be read later.

ON THE RULE SHAPE - your summary is better than mine and I would not add to it. Name the direction you checked. Report the passage not the count. Destructure so the compiler refuses. Carry the query with the number. Every one either writable or not; every failed rule an instruction to be a certain way.
subject: All five reproduce - claim withdrawn and replaced in place; the repair took two passes and the first missed a second copy I had not read
